notes: PART 1 of 2 — merged by tools/generate_pack.py being run on both parts (same pack name; codes continue by track prefix). The state's own OS edition: Louisiana's river, coast, energy, ports and agriculture taught as curriculum, joined by part 2's culture tracks. Facts are public-record Louisiana; transfer checks are phrased against the learner's own parish so they stay true everywhere in the state. 10 tracks x 10 themes x 5 grade bands = 500 blocks total across both parts.

tracks.name: The river: the Mississippi and its machinery

themes.theme: A continent's drain runs past your door
themes.description: The Mississippi's watershed — how water from thirty-one states arrives at Louisiana, and what that makes the river carry.
themes.transfer_check: Trace, on a real map, the path rain falling in two distant states takes to pass Louisiana, and name what it picks up on the way.

bands.K–2: Pour water on a tray of sand and watch where it runs, then find the big river on a map and trace it with your finger to the Gulf.
bands.3–5: On a map of the United States, colour the states whose rain ends up in the Mississippi and trace one raindrop's path past Louisiana.
bands.6–8: Trace, on a real map, the path rain falling in one distant state takes to pass Louisiana, and name two things it picks up on the way.
bands.9–10: Trace, on a real map, the path rain falling in two distant states takes to pass Louisiana, and name what it picks up on the way.
bands.11–12: Trace the paths from two states, quantify one thing the river carries from published measurements, and present the watershed to a class as one system.

themes.description: The mainline levees from the river's own banks — what they protect, what they stopped, and what confining a river costs downstream.
themes.transfer_check: Visit or study the levee section nearest your parish and report who maintains it, its height history, and what sits behind it.

bands.K–2: Stand on or look at a levee with an adult and say what it keeps out and what is behind it.
bands.3–5: Find the levee nearest your parish on a map and draw what it protects on one side and the river on the other.
bands.6–8: Study the levee section nearest your parish and report who maintains it and what sits behind it.
bands.9–10: Visit or study the levee section nearest your parish and report who maintains it, its height history, and what sits behind it.
bands.11–12: Visit the section, report its history and maintainer, and present to a class what confining the river there costs downstream, with sources.

themes.theme: The structures that hold the river in place
themes.description: Old River Control and the spillways — the machinery that keeps the Mississippi in its channel and away from the Atchafalaya's shorter path.
themes.transfer_check: Explain, with a drawing, what Old River Control does and what would change downstream if it failed, verified against an authoritative source.

bands.K–2: Build a channel in sand, let water find a shorter way, and see why people built walls to keep the river where it is.
bands.3–5: Draw the river and the shorter path it wants to take to the Gulf, and mark the structure that stops it.
bands.6–8: Explain, with a drawing, what Old River Control does and what would change downstream if it failed.
bands.9–10: Explain, with a drawing, what Old River Control does and what would change downstream if it failed, verified against an authoritative source.
bands.11–12: Explain the structure from primary sources and lead a class discussion of who would gain and lose if the river moved, with the evidence for each.

themes.description: Bonnet Carré and Morganza — when a spillway opens, who decides, and what the fresh water does to the basins it enters.
themes.transfer_check: From records of one real spillway opening, chart the trigger, the decision-maker, and two documented downstream effects.

bands.K–2: Learn that when the river gets too high, grown-ups open a big gate to let some water out, and draw where it goes.
bands.3–5: Find one time the spillway was opened, and say who decided and where the water went.
bands.6–8: From records of one real spillway opening, chart the trigger and the decision-maker, and name one downstream effect.
bands.9–10: From records of one real spillway opening, chart the trigger, the decision-maker, and two documented downstream effects.
bands.11–12: Compare two openings from the records, explain why the decisions differed, and present the case for and against the second one.

themes.description: River stages, flood stage and the forecast — reading the river's actual numbers the way river communities do.
themes.transfer_check: Read the current stage at the gauge nearest your parish, compare it to flood stage and the record, and state what today's number means.

bands.K–2: Look at a river gauge picture or a real one with an adult and say whether the water is high or low today.
bands.3–5: Read the number at the gauge nearest your parish and put it on a chart against flood stage.
bands.6–8: Read the current stage at the gauge nearest your parish, compare it to flood stage, and say what today's number means.
bands.9–10: Read the current stage at the gauge nearest your parish, compare it to flood stage and the record, and state what today's number means.
bands.11–12: Read the gauge for two weeks, chart it against the forecast, and write the plain-language note a neighbour would need if the trend continued.

themes.theme: The sediment the coast is starving for
themes.description: Mud as treasure — how the leveed river sends land-building sediment off the shelf, and the diversions meant to reclaim it.
themes.transfer_check: Explain the sediment argument for and against one real diversion project, citing each side's own documents.

bands.K–2: Stir mud into water and watch it settle, then learn that the river's mud used to build land at the coast.
bands.3–5: Draw where the river's mud goes now and where a diversion would send it, and say why the coast wants it.
bands.6–8: Explain the sediment argument for one real diversion project from its own documents and one concern raised against it.
bands.9–10: Explain the sediment argument for and against one real diversion project, citing each side's own documents.
bands.11–12: Present both sides of a real diversion to an audience with a stake in it, and record which argument moved them and why.

themes.theme: The river as a working road
themes.description: Tows, barges and pilots — what actually moves on the river, and why one barge tow replaces dozens of trucks.
themes.transfer_check: Observe or study one real stretch of river traffic and report what was moving, in what, and roughly what it would take by road.

bands.K–2: Watch or look at pictures of a barge tow and count the barges, then learn how many trucks that would take.
bands.3–5: Observe or study one stretch of river traffic and say what was moving and in what.
bands.6–8: Observe or study one stretch of river traffic with a checker, report what was moving and in what, and estimate with help what it would take by road.
bands.9–10: Observe or study one real stretch of river traffic and report what was moving, in what, and roughly what it would take by road.
bands.11–12: Observe a stretch of traffic on two days, compute the road equivalent with published figures, and present the river as a highway to a class.

themes.description: The intakes, treatment and saltwater wedge — the communities that drink the Mississippi and what threatens the tap.
themes.transfer_check: Determine whether your own parish drinks river water, and for one that does, trace the intake-to-tap path and its named risks.

bands.K–2: Find out with an adult where your tap water comes from — the river, a well, a lake.
bands.3–5: Find out whether your parish drinks river water and draw the path from the river to the tap.
bands.6–8: Determine whether your parish drinks river water and, for one that does, trace the intake-to-tap path and name one risk.
bands.9–10: Determine whether your own parish drinks river water, and for one that does, trace the intake-to-tap path and its named risks.
bands.11–12: Trace the path, document the named risks from the utility's own reports, and write the resident's note on what a saltwater wedge means for the tap.

themes.description: America's largest river swamp — the basin, its floodway job, and the crawfish economy inside it.
themes.transfer_check: Map the Atchafalaya Basin's floodway role and profile one real livelihood that depends on the basin staying wet.

bands.K–2: Look at pictures of the great swamp and learn that it is where the river would go if it could.
bands.3–5: Find the Atchafalaya Basin on a map, say what it does in a flood, and name one thing people catch there.
bands.6–8: Map the Atchafalaya Basin's floodway role and profile one livelihood that depends on the basin staying wet.
bands.9–10: Map the Atchafalaya Basin's floodway role and profile one real livelihood that depends on the basin staying wet.
bands.11–12: Map the floodway role, profile a livelihood from an interview or its own records, and present what a floodway operation would cost it.

themes.theme: Living in the shadow of the river
themes.description: The capstone: river decisions as parish decisions — levees, diversions, traffic and water, argued with real neighbours.
themes.transfer_check: Run or present a structured deliberation on one real river decision affecting your region, and deliver the recommendation you would defend.

bands.K–2: Talk about one thing the river gives your town and one thing it could take, and say what people do about it.
bands.3–5: Hold a class debate on one real river decision near you and vote.
bands.6–8: Present a structured deliberation on one real river decision affecting your region — options, trade-offs, voices — and give your recommendation.
bands.9–10: Run or present a structured deliberation on one real river decision affecting your region, and deliver the recommendation you would defend.
bands.11–12: Run the deliberation with affected residents in the room, deliver the recommendation to a parish body or class, and record what changed your mind.

tracks.name: The working coast: wetlands and restoration

themes.description: Marsh, swamp, ridge and bayou — reading the coastal landscape's parts and what each does for the state behind it.
themes.transfer_check: Identify marsh, swamp and ridge on real imagery of the Louisiana coast and state one protective job each performs.

bands.K–2: Look at pictures of marsh, swamp and bayou and say which is grass, which is trees, which is water.
bands.3–5: Identify marsh, swamp and ridge on real coast pictures and say one thing each does.
bands.6–8: Identify marsh, swamp and ridge on real imagery of one stretch of the Louisiana coast with a checker, and state one protective job two of them perform.
bands.9–10: Identify marsh, swamp and ridge on real imagery of the Louisiana coast and state one protective job each performs.
bands.11–12: Identify the parts on imagery of your own region, map them, and explain to a class what each does for the town behind it.

themes.description: Coastal land loss — the causes stacked together (subsidence, channels, levees, storms, sea rise) and the honest arithmetic of what is going.
themes.transfer_check: Compare historical and current imagery of one real coastal spot and quantify what has gone, attributing causes from published analysis.

bands.K–2: Look at an old picture and a new picture of the same coast and point to the land that is gone.
bands.3–5: Compare old and new pictures of one coastal spot and say what has gone and one reason why.
bands.6–8: Compare historical and current imagery of one real coastal spot and quantify what has gone, naming one cause from published analysis.
bands.9–10: Compare historical and current imagery of one real coastal spot and quantify what has gone, attributing causes from published analysis.
bands.11–12: Quantify the loss at two spots, attribute the causes with sources, and present the honest arithmetic to a class without a slogan.

themes.description: Surge protection, nurseries and livelihoods — what a mile of marsh is worth to a town it fronts.
themes.transfer_check: For one real coastal community, explain what the fronting wetlands do for it in a storm, citing the protection estimates.

bands.K–2: Build a wall of grass in a tray and see how it slows the water, then learn that marsh does that for towns.
bands.3–5: For one coastal town, say what the marsh in front of it does in a storm.
bands.6–8: For one real coastal community, explain what the fronting wetlands do for it in a storm, citing one protection estimate.
bands.9–10: For one real coastal community, explain what the fronting wetlands do for it in a storm, citing the protection estimates.
bands.11–12: Explain the protection for two communities with different marsh in front of them, and present what losing a mile of it would mean, with sources.

themes.description: The state's fifty-year plan — how projects are chosen, funded and ranked, and how to read it as a citizen.
themes.transfer_check: From the current Master Plan's own documents, summarise the project nearest your parish — type, cost, purpose, status.

bands.K–2: Learn that the state has a big plan to save the coast, and find the project nearest you on the map.
bands.3–5: Find the coastal project nearest your parish in the plan and say what it does.
bands.6–8: From the current Master Plan's documents, summarise the project nearest your parish — type, cost, purpose.
bands.9–10: From the current Master Plan's own documents, summarise the project nearest your parish — type, cost, purpose, status.
bands.11–12: Summarise the nearest project and how it was ranked, and present the plan's choices for your region to a class as a citizen would read them.

themes.description: Dredge, diversion and terrace — the restoration toolbox, what each technique builds, and what each costs.
themes.transfer_check: Match three real restoration projects to their techniques and report what each has measurably built so far.

bands.K–2: Learn the three ways people build new land — pumping mud, opening a diversion, making terraces — and draw one.
bands.3–5: Match three restoration projects to their techniques on a picture card.
bands.6–8: Match three real restoration projects to their techniques and report what one has measurably built so far.
bands.9–10: Match three real restoration projects to their techniques and report what each has measurably built so far.
bands.11–12: Match the projects, report what each built with figures, and compare cost per acre across the three from their own records.

themes.description: Shrimp, oyster, crab and finfish — the working coast's harvest, and how restoration and salinity decisions land on the deck.
themes.transfer_check: Profile one real Louisiana fishery — season, method, landing figures — and one live decision currently affecting it, from both sides.

bands.K–2: Learn what shrimp, oysters and crabs are and that people in Louisiana catch them for a living.
bands.3–5: Profile one Louisiana fishery — when it is in season and how it is caught.
bands.6–8: Profile one real Louisiana fishery — season, method, landing figures — and name one live decision affecting it.
bands.9–10: Profile one real Louisiana fishery — season, method, landing figures — and one live decision currently affecting it, from both sides.
bands.11–12: Profile the fishery, interview or study one person on each side of the decision, and write the balanced brief a council member could use.

themes.theme: The oyster and the salinity line
themes.description: The oyster as an animal with an address — why fresh and salt must balance, and what moves the line.
themes.transfer_check: Explain what a named freshwater event did to a real oyster area, using landings or lease records as evidence.

bands.K–2: Learn that oysters need water that is a little salty, not too fresh, and that the river can change that.
bands.3–5: Explain what happens to an oyster bed when a lot of fresh water comes, using one real example.
bands.6–8: Explain what a named freshwater event did to a real oyster area, using one landings or lease record as evidence.
bands.9–10: Explain what a named freshwater event did to a real oyster area, using landings or lease records as evidence.
bands.11–12: Explain the event with records, and present the trade-off between the freshwater decision and the oyster harvest to an audience with a stake in it.

themes.theme: Communities deciding to stay or go
themes.description: The hardest coastal question — elevation, buyouts and relocation, told through the communities already deciding.
themes.transfer_check: Study one documented Louisiana community's stay-or-move decision and present the options it faced and the choice it made, fairly.

bands.K–2: Hear the story of a coastal town that had to decide whether to move, and say what you would find hardest.
bands.3–5: Study one Louisiana community that decided to stay or move, and say what choices it had.
bands.6–8: Study one documented Louisiana community's stay-or-move decision and present the options it faced, with a checker for fairness.
bands.9–10: Study one documented Louisiana community's stay-or-move decision and present the options it faced and the choice it made, fairly.
bands.11–12: Study two communities that chose differently, present both fairly, and lead a discussion of what your own community would need to decide.

themes.description: The restoration economy — the trades, sciences and boats the Master Plan employs, and the local routes into them.
themes.transfer_check: Map three real jobs on one restoration project — what each does, what it requires — from the project's own records or employers.

bands.K–2: Learn that saving the coast is a job — boats, science, building — and name one.
bands.3–5: Map three jobs on a restoration project and what each person does.
bands.6–8: Map three real jobs on one restoration project — what each does, what it requires — from the project's own records.
bands.9–10: Map three real jobs on one restoration project — what each does, what it requires — from the project's own records or employers.
bands.11–12: Map the jobs, contact one employer or program, and write the route from your parish's high school into one of them.

themes.description: The capstone: reading the projections honestly and arguing what your parish should ask of the plan.
themes.transfer_check: Using the Master Plan's own future maps, describe your region's projected coast and draft your parish's one-page ask of the plan.

bands.K–2: Look at the map of what the coast may look like when you are grown up, and say what you notice.
bands.3–5: Using the plan's future map, describe what your region's coast may look like in fifty years.
bands.6–8: Using the Master Plan's future maps, describe your region's projected coast and draft one ask of the plan.
bands.9–10: Using the Master Plan's own future maps, describe your region's projected coast and draft your parish's one-page ask of the plan.
bands.11–12: Draft the ask, present it to a parish body or class, and revise it from the questions you were asked.

tracks.name: The energy corridor: from well to grid

themes.description: River, feedstock and deep water — the geography that lined the Mississippi with refineries and chemical plants.
themes.transfer_check: For one real corridor facility, explain in a paragraph why it sits where it sits — river, pipeline, port — with evidence.

bands.K–2: Look at a map of the big plants along the river and say why they are next to the water.
bands.3–5: For one plant on the river, say two reasons it is where it is — the river, the pipeline, the port.
bands.6–8: For one real corridor facility, explain in a paragraph why it sits where it sits — river, pipeline, port — with one piece of evidence.
bands.9–10: For one real corridor facility, explain in a paragraph why it sits where it sits — river, pipeline, port — with evidence.
bands.11–12: Explain the siting of two facilities with evidence, and present the corridor's geography to a class as an argument, not a list.

themes.description: Crude in, products out — distillation and units explained at working depth, without the mystery.
themes.transfer_check: Diagram a refinery's main flow from crude to three named products and explain one unit's job to somebody else.

bands.K–2: Learn that a refinery takes thick oil and makes it into fuel and other things, and name two of them.
bands.3–5: Draw the refinery as a box — crude in, three products out — and name the products.
bands.6–8: Diagram a refinery's main flow from crude to three named products and explain one unit's job.
bands.9–10: Diagram a refinery's main flow from crude to three named products and explain one unit's job to somebody else.
bands.11–12: Diagram the flow, explain two units, and teach the whole diagram to a younger learner until they can name the products.

themes.description: Liquefaction, the terminals and the cryogenic chain — why Louisiana became an export coast and what a loading arm does.
themes.transfer_check: Explain the LNG chain from pipeline gas to loaded ship, and locate the terminals on a real map with their parishes named.

bands.K–2: Learn that gas can be made so cold it turns to liquid, and find the big ships that carry it on a map.
bands.3–5: Find Louisiana's LNG terminals on a map and say what parish each is in.
bands.6–8: Explain the LNG chain from pipeline gas to loaded ship, and locate two terminals on a real map with their parishes named.
bands.9–10: Explain the LNG chain from pipeline gas to loaded ship, and locate the terminals on a real map with their parishes named.
bands.11–12: Explain the chain, locate the terminals, and present one terminal's economic and community record from primary documents.

themes.description: The buried network — how pipelines are marked, mapped and struck, and the call made before any digging.
themes.transfer_check: Use the official locator process for a real or staged dig on a real parcel, and read the pipeline markers nearest your parish.

bands.K–2: Learn that pipes run under the ground and that grown-ups call a number before they dig.
bands.3–5: Find pipeline markers near your school or home with an adult and learn what the call-before-you-dig number is.
bands.6–8: Use the official locator process for a staged dig on a real parcel, and read the pipeline markers nearest your parish.
bands.9–10: Use the official locator process for a real or staged dig on a real parcel, and read the pipeline markers nearest your parish.
bands.11–12: Run the locator process for a real dig, document the response, and write the card a homeowner could follow before planting a tree.

themes.description: The maintenance surges that employ thousands — what a turnaround is, the crafts it calls, and how workers plug in.
themes.transfer_check: Profile one real turnaround's scale and crafts from public sources, and map how a qualified local worker actually gets hired onto one.

bands.K–2: Learn that big plants stop sometimes for many people to fix them, like a giant repair day.
bands.3–5: Find out what a turnaround is and name three kinds of workers it needs.
bands.6–8: Profile one real turnaround's scale and crafts from public sources, and map one way a qualified local worker gets hired onto one.
bands.9–10: Profile one real turnaround's scale and crafts from public sources, and map how a qualified local worker actually gets hired onto one.
bands.11–12: Profile the turnaround, interview or study one worker's route in, and write the guide from a parish trade hall to a turnaround job.

themes.description: Living next to industry — monitoring, alerts, shelter-in-place, and the community's lawful levers on permits.
themes.transfer_check: For one real fence-line community, find its monitoring data and alert system, and demonstrate the shelter-in-place response.

bands.K–2: Learn that people who live next to a plant have a way to know if something is wrong, and practise going inside and shutting the windows.
bands.3–5: For one community next to a plant, find where its alerts come from and practise shelter-in-place at home.
bands.6–8: For one real fence-line community, find its monitoring data and alert system, and demonstrate shelter-in-place.
bands.9–10: For one real fence-line community, find its monitoring data and alert system, and demonstrate the shelter-in-place response.
bands.11–12: Find the data and alerts, demonstrate the response, and present the community's lawful levers on a permit from the agency's own process.

themes.theme: The safety culture that keeps hands
themes.description: Process safety, permits-to-work and the refusal that is a duty — the corridor's safety systems as working practice.
themes.transfer_check: Walk a staged permit-to-work for a simple task — hazards named, isolations listed, sign-offs in order — and name the stop-work right.

bands.K–2: Learn that at big plants everyone can say stop when something is unsafe, and practise saying it.
bands.3–5: Walk a simple task through the safety questions — what could hurt, what is turned off, who signs.
bands.6–8: Walk a staged permit-to-work for a simple task with a checker — hazards named, isolations listed, sign-offs in order — and name the stop-work right.
bands.9–10: Walk a staged permit-to-work for a simple task — hazards named, isolations listed, sign-offs in order — and name the stop-work right.
bands.11–12: Write and run the permit-to-work for a real hall task, teach the stop-work right to a group, and record one stop that was called.

themes.theme: The grid the plants and parishes share
themes.description: Generation, the big substations and hurricane hardening — Louisiana's electricity from plant to parish line.
themes.transfer_check: Trace your parish's power from its likely generation source through one named substation, and report the utility's storm-hardening work there.

bands.K–2: Learn that electricity comes from a big plant to your house through wires, and find a substation on the way.
bands.3–5: Trace your parish's electricity from a likely plant to a substation to your street on a map.
bands.6–8: Trace your parish's power from its likely generation source through one named substation, and note one storm-hardening measure.
bands.9–10: Trace your parish's power from its likely generation source through one named substation, and report the utility's storm-hardening work there.
bands.11–12: Trace the power, report the hardening from the utility's filings, and present what a named storm did to your parish's grid and what changed after.

themes.description: Hydrogen, carbon capture and offshore wind — the projects actually proposed here, read without slogans.
themes.transfer_check: Take one real announced transition project in Louisiana and examine its claims, funding and status from primary documents.

bands.K–2: Learn that people are building new kinds of energy on the river — wind, hydrogen — and name one.
bands.3–5: Find one new energy project announced in Louisiana and say what it claims it will do.
bands.6–8: Take one real announced transition project in Louisiana and examine its claims and status from primary documents.
bands.9–10: Take one real announced transition project in Louisiana and examine its claims, funding and status from primary documents.
bands.11–12: Examine two projects from primary documents, compare claims with status, and present a balanced brief without slogans.

themes.description: The capstone: process tech, crafts and the two-year path — mapping a real corridor career from a parish high school.
themes.transfer_check: Map one complete real route from your parish's high school to a named corridor job — program, cost, credential, starting pay — from the providers' own information.

bands.K–2: Name one job at a plant on the river and one thing a person learns to do it.
bands.3–5: Map one route from your school to a plant job — the class, the program, the first job.
bands.6–8: Map one real route from your parish's high school to a named corridor job — program, cost, credential — from the providers' own information.
bands.9–10: Map one complete real route from your parish's high school to a named corridor job — program, cost, credential, starting pay — from the providers' own information.
bands.11–12: Map two routes, contact one provider, and write the guide a counsellor could hand to a student in your parish.

themes.theme: The port complex nobody sees whole
themes.description: From Baton Rouge to the Gulf — the string of ports that together move more tonnage than almost anywhere, and what each handles.
themes.transfer_check: Name the major Louisiana ports on a real map with each one's main cargo, citing the ports' own figures.

bands.K–2: Look at pictures of the big ships on the river and learn that Louisiana's ports move more than almost anywhere.
bands.3–5: Find the major Louisiana ports on a map and say what one of them mostly handles.
bands.6–8: Name the major Louisiana ports on a real map with each one's main cargo, citing the ports' own figures for two of them.

bands.11–12: Explain the chain with figures, and present what a low-river year does to it from the records of one such year.

bands.9–10: Describe the pilotage handoffs a ship makes from the Gulf to Baton Rouge and what each pilot group's charge covers.

bands.K–2: Learn that the river fills with mud and that big machines dig it out so ships can pass.
bands.3–5: Find out how deep the river channel is kept and what a dredge does.
